Green #hydrogen is projected to be able to reach 7-8% of final energy demand by 2050, more than double the needs of the entire shipping sector today.

But hydrogen must complement—never replace—development objectives.
 
At today’s #COP30 dialogue organized by the Council of Engineers for the Energy Transition and Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL) , I steered the discussion to explore how to ensure green hydrogen supports national development priorities, protects ecosystems, and creates shared prosperity.

1️⃣ Align hydrogen with national development priorities:
When tied to national strategies, these investments can decarbonize hard-to-abate sectors and build local industry and energy security. Without this, they risk becoming extractive, with value exported and impacts retained.

2️⃣ Strengthen governance across the land–water–energy system
Hydrogen is not a standalone investment—it depends on water resources, land availability, and grid capacity. In Namibia, a 2-million-tonne project would require 18 million m³ of water annually, equivalent to the needs of more than 250,000 people. Countries need integrated planning, clear regulation, and national innovation systems.

3️⃣ Ensure hydrogen creates local prosperity, not only export pathways:
Not every country can or should pursue large-scale hydrogen. The right pathway depends on water availability, land constraints, energy access needs, and industrial priorities.  Where hydrogen is viable, it must deliver domestic value: but in local jobs, resilient value chains, and equitable benefits.

These priorities underpin the UNDP –TIDE Centre, University of Oxford report “Navigating the Currents of Green Hydrogen”, which introduces a People–Planet–Prosperity framework to help countries determine where hydrogen adds genuine value: 🔗📘 bit.ly/Green-H2
